strengths: The task is well motivated: distinguishing and tracking individual sounding objects extends audio-visual semantic segmentation in a meaningful way. Figure 1 clearly illustrates the distinction, with potential applications in video editing and multimodal scene understanding.

AVISeg provides a concrete initial resource: 117 annotated videos containing 6,973 frames, 281 objects, and 15,355 masks. The larger collection includes 26 categories and substantially longer recordings than the cited AVSBench setting, while Figure 2 illustrates varied scenes and changing sound-source activity.

The spatiotemporal IoU formulation in Eq. (2), together with standard VIS AP and AR, appropriately evaluates segmentation and temporal association jointly. Table 1 establishes initial reference results of 31.5 AP with ResNet-50 and 35.6 AP with Swin-Base.

Combining Mask2Former, VGGish, TPAVI, and audio-conditioned queries is a plausible baseline design. The paper appropriately presents this as an initial method, and supplies useful training details including optimizer settings, iterations, batch size, and hardware.
weaknesses: The decisive experimental gap is the absence of evidence that predictions depend meaningfully on audio. Table 1 compares only two visual backbones within the same multimodal model. A visual-only Mask2Former comparison and muted or shuffled audio controls are missing, as are ablations of TPAVI and the audio queries. Consequently, the reported scores cannot establish whether the benchmark rewards auditory grounding beyond visual appearance and category cues. This directly affects validation of the proposed task.

The annotation protocol is insufficiently specified for the central dataset contribution. Section 3 describes SAM-assisted masking but does not explain how annotators determine which instance produces a sound, resolve ambiguous mixtures, mark sound onset and offset, or preserve identities through silent intervals. No annotation audit or agreement evidence supports the asserted high quality. Accurate object contours alone do not establish correct audio-to-instance attribution.

The demonstrated benchmark is substantially smaller than the collected pool: only 117 of 1,258 videos are annotated, with 84 training and 33 testing videos. Figure 3 describes the collection rather than establishing class coverage in these splits. The selection and splitting procedure, source-video separation, and frequency of simultaneous same-class sources are unspecified. With no results broken down by sound-source configuration or video length, the evidence does not establish how well the annotated subset exercises the advertised diversity and long-term challenges. Dataset size alone would not determine rejection, but these missing details limit interpretation of the results.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Section 4.2 does not explain how the time-indexed learnable instance queries maintain identities or accommodate variable-length inference after training with T = 2. Eq. (1) leaves the contractions and projections needed for its residual addition unspecified. Audio-window alignment and whether video-level matching and losses are inherited unchanged are also unclear. Referencing Mask2Former helps, but the manuscript provides no dataset/code access information or exact split identifiers to resolve these reproducibility gaps.

Presentation issues are secondary: Section 5.2 describes Figure 6 as columns of raw frames, ground truth, and predictions, whereas the figure uses temporal columns and unlabeled comparison rows. These correctable issues do not drive the recommendation. Overall, the useful task formulation and initial annotations merit recognition, but unresolved benchmark validity and missing evidence of audio-dependent behavior currently favor weak rejection.
